claims.statement: For the stated binary-CSP formulation, maintain one domain value for each variable. Select a variable currently in conflict with at least one other variable, and evaluate its possible values against the other current assignments. Choose a minimum-conflict value, breaking ties randomly. The current value remains an eligible candidate, so an update can leave the assignment unchanged or move sideways. Initialization and the choice among conflicted variables belong to the surrounding search strategy. In the described local-repair use, repeat repairs until a consistent assignment is found or a chosen budget ends. The same value-ordering idea can instead guide an informed backtracking procedure; that procedure is not an exact synonym for the heuristic.

entries.name: Breakout method
entries.definition: A finite constraint-satisfaction search method that takes strictly improving local assignment changes under a weighted nogood cost and increases the weights of all currently violated nogoods at a non-solution local minimum to change the search landscape.
entries.identity_notes: This is Morris’s Breakout method, using weights on forbidden assignment tuples, not the Breakout game. It is distinct from the idealized Fill algorithm, which raises only the current state’s stored cost, and from GLS, which selects features by penalty utility. Shared adaptive-penalty ideas do not make Breakout, GENET and GLS exact synonyms. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 310 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 3 and 9 lines respectively. All twelve text hits were inspected: six prior candidate-lead lines across the checkouts and six unrelated Pygments lexer-state lines in the ignored main environment. No hit established an existing candidate record. Seven exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and five native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The practical Breakout method is incomplete. The paper supplies a satisfiable four-variable CNF counterexample where repeated reweighting can oscillate without reaching the all-true solution. No finite-budget success or unsatisfiability certificate is implied.

The paper’s completeness theorem applies to the distinct idealized Fill algorithm, which stores and raises the cost of the current state alone on the finite assignment space. It must not be transferred to Breakout’s shared nogood weights.

Representation affects the penalty landscape: one constraint can contain several forbidden tuples, and shared nogoods couple costs of different assignments. A constraint-weight implementation requires evidence that its intended representation matches this scope.

Random initialization is an experimental choice, not a required random restart after each local minimum. Favorable results on constructed distributions do not establish general efficiency. The finite curator calculation checks a prefix of the published counterexample, not an independent proof for infinite executions.

claims.statement: Represent forbidden assignment tuples as nogoods, give each weight1, and score a complete assignment by the sum of weights of the nogoods it matches. Until a satisfying assignment is reached, make any local assignment change that strictly lowers this weighted cost when one exists. At a non-solution local minimum, increment every currently matched nogood’s weight by1 and repeat the search/weight-increase cycle until an improving move becomes available. Plateau points are treated as local minima rather than traversed by unweighted sideways moves. The method leaves initialization and the choice among improving changes open; the reported implementation uses random initial assignments and the first improving change found in a left-to-right scan. Weight increases persist and can also raise costs of neighboring states sharing the same nogoods.

entries.name: GSAT
entries.definition: A randomized local-search SAT procedure that repeatedly flips a Boolean variable giving the largest change toward more satisfied CNF clauses, breaks tied choices randomly, and restarts from a random complete assignment under specified flip and attempt budgets.
entries.identity_notes: This is the Selman–Levesque–Mitchell GSAT model-finding procedure. It evaluates single-variable flips across the current assignment, rather than first choosing a conflicted variable and then its minimum-conflict domain value. It is not strict hill climbing, a resolution proof procedure, a generic language-model reasoner or every later GSAT/WalkSAT extension. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 310 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 3 and 9 lines respectively. All twelve text hits were inspected: six prior candidate-lead lines across the checkouts and six unrelated Pygments lexer-state lines in the ignored main environment. No hit established an existing candidate record. Seven exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and five native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: GSAT is an incomplete model finder under finite budgets. A satisfiable formula may be missed, and the source discusses families that can require exponentially many attempts. Search failure must not be reported as an UNSAT proof.
Allowing plateau and occasionally decreasing flips distinguishes the method from strict-improvement hill climbing. Replacing these moves with immediate restarts changes the specified procedure.

The Figure1 pre-flip test leaves a final-flip boundary: with one allowed flip on a single positive unit clause, an initially false assignment can become satisfying after the last check. The record exposes this literal pseudocode behavior rather than silently certifying a corrected implementation.

MAX-FLIPS, MAX-TRIES, randomization, tie handling and CNF encoding affect outcomes. Experiments on selected satisfiable instances and particular distributions are not universal runtime or success guarantees; no numerical benchmark result is curated.

claims.statement: For up to MAX-TRIES attempts, generate a random complete truth assignment for the input CNF clauses. During each attempt, test the current assignment for satisfaction and, while within MAX-FLIPS, choose a variable whose flip gives the largest increase in the number of satisfied clauses, breaking equally good choices randomly, then flip it. The argmax does not require a positive gain: sideways moves remain possible, and the source also acknowledges occasional decreasing moves. Restart after the per-attempt budget and report search failure after all attempts if no tested satisfying assignment was found. A returned assignment is a directly checkable model; an unsuccessful search does not prove unsatisfiability. Figure1 checks before each flip, so the assignment produced by the last allowed flip is not checked inside its literal loop; a concrete implementation must state whether it adds that final check.

If every utility is zero, the all-feature pseudocode makes absent features tie with present ones, whereas the prose says only local-minimum features are penalized. A concrete implementation must declare its zero-utility and eligible-feature convention; the record’s stated update is restricted to the positive-maximum case.

Curator qualification of Equation 1: equal penalties contribute lambda*p times the number of active features. They cancel from move-cost differences only when that feature count is unchanged. The source’s equal-penalty cancellation statement is therefore not universal for variable-cardinality feature sets.

Penalties are finite soft costs, not hard prohibitions. Their effect depends on lambda, objective scale, feature definition, move set and stopping. At lambda=0 the guidance vanishes; increasing penalties does not prove escape from every basin or convergence to a global optimum.

Local minima are relative to h and the chosen neighborhood, not necessarily g. claims.statement: Choose binary indicators I_i(s) for nontrivial solution features, feature costs c_i, a local-search procedure and penalty scale lambda. In the inspected basic formulation the c_i are fixed and nonnegative, and penalties p_i start at zero. Repeatedly run local search from the current solution using h(s)=g(s)+lambda*sum_i p_i*I_i(s), where g is the original cost. At an h-local minimum s_star, compute u_i=I_i(s_star)*c_i/(1+p_i). In the nondegenerate case of positive maximum utility, increment p_i by one for every feature tied at that maximum, then resume local search from the same solution under the modified h. Penalization can repeat without an intervening move. Feature costs enter the utility ranking, not as extra multipliers in the displayed penalty sum. Retain and return the best solution found according to g, rather than choosing it by the changing augmented objective. FLS and other accelerations may be combined with the local-search subroutine but are not required by this baseline.

native_neighbors.name: Simulated annealing
native_neighbors.definition: A stochastic optimization procedure that explores candidate configurations with temperature-controlled acceptance of cost-increasing moves and progressively cools that acceptance process to concentrate search on low-cost configurations.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes the temperature-scheduled optimization procedure exemplified by Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi. Its basic symmetric-proposal Metropolis step is distinguished from fixed-temperature target sampling, generic annealing metaphors, training signal annealing and a proof that a particular finite schedule reaches a global minimum. The 1983 article is a primary formulation, not a claim of exclusive invention. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 285 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 15 and 15 lines respectively. Every text hit was a prior candidate lead. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and seven native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The exp(−delta/T) expression is for positive effective temperature with the physical Boltzmann constant absorbed into its cost units. Zero temperature is a limiting or separately defined greedy rule, not evaluation of that quotient at T=0. Equal-cost moves are accepted in the displayed symmetric-proposal rule.

At fixed T the Boltzmann interpretation requires a proper target and a valid transition construction. Arbitrary asymmetric proposals do not justify dropping the reverse-to-forward proposal ratio. Lowering T changes the target; stationarity for a fixed stage does not imply equilibrium throughout a finite cooling run.

Positive-temperature uphill acceptance only permits escape through moves supported by the proposal. It does not ensure reaching every state, escaping a local basin in a chosen budget or tracking equilibrium. Rapid cooling can freeze search prematurely; schedule length, cost scale, move connectivity and constraints matter.

The primary article’s heuristics and empirical scaling claims are not a finite-run global-convergence theorem or a universal complexity bound. The later mathematical conditions for asymptotic annealing convergence were not audited here. No electronic-design or traveling-salesman benchmark is reproduced.

claims.statement: Choose a representation of feasible configurations, an objective E to minimize, a random rearrangement proposal and an annealing schedule specifying temperatures and work at each temperature. For the basic symmetric-proposal Metropolis rule at effective temperature T>0 measured in cost units, accept delta<=0 moves and accept delta>0 with probability exp(−delta/T); otherwise retain x. Repeat transitions at the current temperature, then lower temperature according to the schedule. High temperatures permit larger cost-increasing moves more frequently; cooling reduces that probability. The source motivates sufficient equilibration at each stage. Candidate representation, move set and schedule depend on the optimization problem; the returned low-cost configuration is a search result rather than a certified global minimizer.
